orthography: ALMY 1984 standardized alphabet: ' for glottal stop and ejectives (k', ch', ts', p', t'), doubled vowels for length, tone not marked. Where modern sources (Bricker et al. 1998; 2014 SEGEY/INALI norms) write high tone with an acute accent (e.g. báalam, k'áak'nab), the note or headword gives that spelling; reviewers decide whether the deck marks tone. x = [ʃ], j = [h], ch = [tʃ]. LOANWORD POLICY: Spanish loans keep standard Spanish spelling (cóndor, martillo, cristal, piña), never invented respellings; IPA for loans gives the Spanish pronunciation. IPA is broad, has no tone, and a '?' in the note marks an uncertain transcription.
status: DRAFT for native-speaker review. Not approved. Do not ship as authoritative (PRD §1 goal 5, §3.1).

jaguar.headword: báalam (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
jaguar.note: Changed from existing draft 'balam' (colonial/Classic spelling) to show the long vowel of modern Yucatec, written báalam with tone in Bricker et al. 1998 and Bastarrachea et al. Diccionario básico. Alternative: chak mo'ol (also cited for jaguar/puma; regional). Association: balamo'ob are also guardian spirits of milpa and village in traditional belief; the animal sense is ordinary everyday usage, but reviewers should confirm it reads as the animal for children.

colibri.headword: ts'unu'un (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
colibri.note: Kept existing draft. Widely documented (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico; Cordemex). Tone/length marking varies across sources (ts'unu'un vs ts'úunu'un).

llama.reviewQuestion: For the Andean llama, do you use a Maya word or just say 'llama'? How do you pronounce it?
llama.note: Spanish loanword. The llama is Andean and not native to the peninsula; no traditional Yucatec word is expected. Medium only because it is clearly a loan; Spanish spelling kept per loan policy; pronunciation may be [jama]. Do not invent a native term. Alternative to review: keep Spanish spelling as a marked loan.

condor.reviewQuestion: Do you have any word for the condor, or would you say 'cóndor' (or something like nojoch ch'oom, 'big vulture')?
condor.note: Spanish loan (cóndor), kept in Spanish spelling per loan policy. Andean bird, not native to the region. Alternative descriptive: nojoch ch'oom 'big vulture' (nojoch 'big' + ch'oom 'vulture/zopilote', both attested), which is transparent but not an established name.

mariposa.headword: péepem (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
mariposa.note: Standard word, written péepem with tone (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico). Also used for moths.

guajolote.headword: úulum (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
guajolote.note: úulum = domestic turkey (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex ulum). The wild ocellated turkey of the peninsula is kuuts, a different bird; the card shows the gobbling domestic turkey. Association: turkeys are offered in some traditional ceremonies; the word itself is everyday.

tortuga.headword: áak (Cordemex ac) (from memory; page not verified)
tortuga.reviewQuestion: How do you say 'turtle': áak, aak, or ak? Is the vowel long? Could a child confuse it with áaktun (cave) or p'aak (tomato) when called aloud?
tortuga.note: áak 'turtle' (Cordemex; Bricker et al. 1998). Risk: near-homophones on this deck (aaktun cave, p'aak tomato) and elsewhere (ak' 'vine'); reviewers should confirm vowel length and the plain vs ejective k. Species names exist for sea vs land turtles; this is the general term. IPA ?.

rana.headword: much (Diccionario básico) (from memory; page not verified)
rana.reviewQuestion: Is 'much' only a toad, or also a green frog like this picture? What do you call a green frog? Is wo' fine for children or tied to the rain ceremony?
rana.note: much is the common word for toad, used loosely for frogs (Diccionario básico; Bricker); it may not cover the green frog of the card, hence low. wo' (uo), a rain-singing frog, is avoided as the card word because wo' frogs are part of the Ch'a' Cháak rain ceremony, where children imitate their calls.

serpiente.headword: kàan (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
serpiente.note: kàan/káan 'snake' (Bricker et al. 1998). Do not confuse with ka'an 'sky' (glottal stop) or kaan 'four' in some spellings. Association: the feathered serpent K'uk'ulkan; the plain word is everyday.

maiz.headword: ixi'im (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
maiz.note: Kept existing draft. Standard word for maize grain (all major dictionaries). Related: nal 'ear of corn (fresh)'. Maize carries deep cultural and ritual weight, but ixi'im is the ordinary noun.

nopal.headword: pak'am (Cordemex pakam) (from memory; page not verified)
nopal.reviewQuestion: How do you say 'nopal': pak'am or pak'an? Is it used for the plant, the fruit (tuna), or both?
nopal.note: pak'am (also pak'an) 'nopal, tuna' in Cordemex and Diccionario básico. Final m vs n varies by source; reviewers should confirm. Opuntia occurs on the peninsula but is less culturally central than in central Mexico. IPA ?.

frijol.headword: bu'ul (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
frijol.note: Kept existing draft. Standard word (all major dictionaries). Specific varieties have their own names (e.g. ib 'lima bean').

pina.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for pineapple, or do people just say 'piña'?
pina.note: Spanish loanword. I could not confirm a native Yucatec name for pineapple from sources I trust; rather than guess, this is left as a marked loan. Colonial dictionaries may record a native term; a reviewer should check Cordemex. Spanish spelling kept per loan policy.

chile.headword: ìik (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
chile.note: ìik/iik 'chile' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico), as in x-ma'ax iik. Minimal pair with iik' 'wind' (ejective k') on the viento card; callers must pronounce the ejective clearly, and reviewers may want to flag this pair for children.

papa.reviewQuestion: Do people say 'papa' for potato in Maya, or another word?
papa.note: Spanish loanword. Potato is Andean; no traditional Yucatec name expected. Do not substitute iis, which is sweet potato (camote), a different plant.

aguacate.headword: óon (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
aguacate.note: óon 'avocado' (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex on). Short, may need a clear call.

tomate.headword: p'aak (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
tomate.note: p'aak 'tomato' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico). Native word.

girasol.reviewQuestion: What do you call a sunflower? Would 'u lool k'iin' sound natural, strange, or wrong?
girasol.note: Built from attested roots: u (3rd person possessive) + lool 'flower' + k'iin 'sun'. Not an established name. Sunflower is not a traditional peninsular crop; speakers most likely say girasol (Spanish loan), which is a safe alternative. The possessive phrase order should be checked by a speaker. IPA ?.

sol.headword: k'iin (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
sol.note: Kept existing draft. k'iin = sun, day, time (all major dictionaries). Association: K'inich, solar deity; the plain noun is everyday. Respectful address forms (e.g. Yuum K'iin) avoided.

luna.headword: uj (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
luna.note: Kept existing draft. uj = moon, month (all major dictionaries). Some speakers use respectful/ritual address forms for the moon; those are avoided here.

estrella.headword: éek' (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
estrella.note: éek' 'star' (Bricker et al. 1998; Diccionario básico). Do not confuse with ek' 'black, dark' in some colonial spellings.

lluvia.reviewQuestion: What is the everyday word for 'rain' (the noun): ja'al, ja'ajal, cháak, or something else? Is cháak acceptable for children, or only for the rain deity?
lluvia.note: Changed from ja'ajal (reviewer flagged it unverified; it may be the verb 'to rain'). ja'al is offered as the noun 'rain', derived from ja' 'water'; IPA ? and form unverified. Deliberately avoided: cháak, which can mean rain in everyday speech but is also the name of the rain deity (Ch'a' Cháak ceremony); if speakers say cháak for rain the owner must decide whether that is acceptable.

rayo.reviewQuestion: What do you call a lightning flash in everyday speech? Is 'lelem' right, and is the word connected to the Chaako'ob in a way that should stay off a children's game?
rayo.note: lelem 'lightning, flash' as I recall it from Cordemex (cf. lemba' 'to shine'); kept as attested only on that recollection, with low confidence: I cannot confirm it is the everyday modern word. IPA ?. Association: lightning is tied to the Chaako'ob (rain deities) and their axes; avoid any form naming them.

arcoiris.headword: chéel (Cordemex chel) (from memory; page not verified)
arcoiris.reviewQuestion: What do you call a rainbow? Is 'chéel' right? Is the rainbow considered dangerous or unlucky, and would it be OK on a children's card?
arcoiris.note: PROVISIONAL. chéel 'rainbow' as recalled from Cordemex/Bricker; I am not sure of the form or that it is in everyday use, so confidence is low. Taboo risk: in some communities the rainbow is considered dangerous (said to come out of cenotes, cause illness, not to be pointed at), and it is linked in scholarship with Ix Chel. A speaker must confirm it is acceptable on a children's card.

nube.headword: múuyal (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

viento.headword: iik' (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
viento.note: iik' 'wind, breath' (all major dictionaries). Also means spirit/breath and is a day name in the calendar; the everyday sense is wind. Minimal pair with iik 'chile' (plain k) on the chile card.

cometa.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a comet? Would 'búuts' éek'' (smoke star) be understood, or do people say 'cometa'?
cometa.note: búuts' 'smoke' (long vowel, as in Bricker et al. 1998) + éek' 'star'. Earlier draft wrote short buts'. I believe colonial dictionaries record budz ek for comet, which would make it attested, but I have not verified it, so it is descriptive, low. Alternative: Spanish loan cometa.

montana.headword: wits (Cordemex witz) (from memory; page not verified)
montana.reviewQuestion: Is 'wits' the word for a big mountain, or only for a hill? Would you use puuk?
montana.note: wits (colonial witz) 'hill, mountain' (Cordemex; Bricker). The peninsula is flat; locally the word mostly names hills. Alternative: puuk 'range of hills' (the Puuc). Snowy peaks in the verse have no local referent.

volcan.reviewQuestion: How would you say 'volcano'? Would 'k'aak'il wits' (fire mountain) make sense, or do people just say 'volcán'?
volcan.note: Built from k'aak' 'fire' + -il (relational suffix) + wits 'hill/mountain'. There are no volcanoes on the peninsula and no traditional word is expected; Spanish volcán is the likely everyday form and a safe alternative. Modifier construction needs a speaker's check (k'aak' wits vs k'aak'il wits). IPA ?.

manantial.reviewQuestion: What do you call a spring where water comes out of the ground? Is 'sayab' a word you know or use?
manantial.note: sayab 'manantial, ojo de agua' (Cordemex). Its everyday modern use is uncertain. Alternative culturally central water source: ts'ono'ot 'cenote', but that is a sinkhole, a different referent, and cenotes have strong ritual associations; not used. Lowered to low: I recall sayab from Cordemex but not its modern currency.

mar.headword: k'áak'nab (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)

desierto.reviewQuestion: How would you say 'desert'? Would 'tikin lu'um' (dry land) make sense, or do people say 'desierto'?
desierto.note: tikin 'dry' + lu'um 'earth, land', both attested. No deserts on the peninsula; not an established term. Spanish desierto is a likely everyday alternative. IPA ?.

selva.headword: k'áax (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
selva.note: k'áax 'forest, wild land, monte' (all major dictionaries). Covers scrub forest broadly, not only tall jungle. The verse's monkeys fit (ma'ax 'spider monkey').

cristal.reviewQuestion: Do you say 'cristal' for a rock crystal? Is there a Maya word that is NOT the sáastun of the j-meen?
cristal.note: Spanish loan, kept in Spanish spelling per loan policy. Deliberately avoided: sáastun 'clear stone', the divining crystal used by the j-meen (traditional ritual specialist), a sacred object. Also avoided sáasil tuunich 'clear stone' for being too close to it.

isla.reviewQuestion: Do people today say 'peten' for an island, or mostly 'isla'?
isla.note: peten 'island' (Cordemex; source of the place name Petén). Well attested historically; reviewers should confirm current everyday use versus Spanish isla.

cueva.headword: áaktun (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
cueva.note: áaktun (colonial actun) 'cave' (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex). Association: caves are traditional offering places and entrances to the underworld in belief; the noun itself is everyday (common in place names).

olla.reviewQuestion: What do you call a clay cooking pot: kum or kuum? Is it different from p'uul?
olla.note: kum/kuum 'olla' (Cordemex; Diccionario básico). Vowel length uncertain across sources. Related: p'uul 'water jar (cántaro)', a different vessel. IPA ?.

cesto.headword: xúuxak (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
cesto.reviewQuestion: What do you call a woven basket: xúuxak, xak, or something else? Is the vowel long?
cesto.note: Kept xúuxak over xak: my recollection is that xúuxak is the modern basket word and xak the colonial form (Cordemex xac), but I am not sure; low. Length ?. IPA ?.

tambor.reviewQuestion: What do you call a drum like this one (hit with hands or sticks)? Is 'tunkul' / 'tunk'ul' that drum, or only the hollow log drum? Is it tied to ceremonies?
tambor.note: tunkul / tunk'ul (colonial spelling tunkul) is the hollow-log slit drum (cf. Nahuatl teponaztli). Uncertain: plain vs ejective k, and whether it fits a hand drum. The skin drum is pax/paax in some sources, but paax now commonly means 'music'. Association: used in traditional ceremonies and dances. IPA ?.

adobe.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a mud brick, or do people say 'adobe'?
adobe.note: Spanish loan. Adobe is not a traditional peninsular building material (houses are stone, bajareque/wattle-and-daub, and palm thatch), so no native term is expected. Descriptive alternative for review: luk' tuunich 'mud stone' (luk' 'mud' + tuunich 'stone'), not established.

hilo.headword: k'u'uch (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
hilo.reviewQuestion: What do you call cotton thread: k'u'uch, k'uuch, or something else?
hilo.note: k'u'uch 'thread, spun cotton' (Bricker et al. 1998; Cordemex). Related: piits' 'cotton' (raw). Glottal placement needs confirmation. Lowered to low: form and glottal placement unverified. IPA ?.

canoa.reviewQuestion: Do people still say 'chem' for a canoe or small boat?
canoa.note: chem 'canoe, boat' (Cordemex; Bricker). Well attested historically; reviewers should confirm everyday use (some speakers may say barco or kanoa for boats).

puente.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a bridge, or do people say 'puente'?
puente.note: Spanish loan, likely the everyday form in a region with few rivers. I could not confirm a native everyday word. Colonial dictionaries may record a term (to check in Cordemex). Do not invent one.

vela.headword: kib (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
vela.note: kib 'wax, candle' (all major dictionaries). Association: candles are central to offerings (e.g. Janal Pixan, Day of the Dead) but the word is everyday.

martillo.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a hammer, or do people say 'martillo'?
martillo.note: Spanish loan, kept in Spanish spelling per loan policy (earlier draft respelling 'martiyo' removed as unsourced). Related native verb: baj 'to hammer, nail in' (Bricker), but I do not know a native tool noun.

casa.headword: naj (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
casa.note: naj/naaj 'house' (all major dictionaries; length varies by source). Alternative: otoch 'home', usually possessed (in wotoch 'my home').

milpa.headword: kool (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
milpa.note: kool 'milpa' (all major dictionaries). Spanish milpa is not from Maya (it is from Nahuatl). Association: milpa ceremonies (e.g. jaanli kool) exist but kool itself is ordinary.

tienda.reviewQuestion: What do you call the corner shop: 'tienda', 'kúuchil koonol', or something else?
tienda.note: kúuchil 'place' + koonol 'selling' (kon 'to sell'), both attested. Transparent phrase, not confirmed as the usual word; many speakers likely say tienda (Spanish loan), a safe alternative. IPA ?.

plaza.headword: k'íiwik (Cordemex kiuic) (from memory; page not verified)
plaza.reviewQuestion: What do you call the town square: k'íiwik, or 'plaza'? Long vowel?
plaza.note: k'íiwik (colonial kiuic) 'plaza, market' (Cordemex; Bricker). Vowel length and ejective need confirmation. IPA ?.

puerto.reviewQuestion: Is there a Maya word for a harbour, or do people say 'puerto'?
puerto.note: Spanish loan, likely the everyday form (cf. place names Puerto Progreso, Puerto Morelos). Descriptive alternative for review: u kúuchil chem 'place of the canoes' (kúuchil 'place' + chem 'canoe'), not established.

pueblo.headword: kaaj (Bricker et al. 1998) (from memory; page not verified)
pueblo.note: kaaj/kaj 'town, community' (all major dictionaries; Restall's work on the colonial cah). Length varies by source.

escuela.reviewQuestion: Do people say 'escuela' in Maya, or 'najil xook' / another phrase?
escuela.note: Changed from descriptive naajil xook. I believe speakers mostly say escuela, and naajil xook is too close to naaj (casa) for a three-choice call. Alternative for review: naajil xook 'house of reading/study' (naaj 'house' + -il + xook 'read, study'), which I believe appears in bilingual-education materials but cannot cite.

observatorio.reviewQuestion: Do people say 'observatorio', or is there a Maya way to say 'a place to watch the stars'?
observatorio.note: Spanish loan; modern institution with no traditional word. Kept as loan (not a naajil- phrase, to avoid clashing with naaj on casa). Descriptive alternative for review: naajil u cha'anta'al eek'o'ob 'house where the stars are watched' (cha'an 'to watch', eek' 'star', -o'ob plural), grammar unverified. Note El Caracol at Chichén Itzá is popularly called an observatory, but that name is Spanish.

biblioteca.reviewQuestion: Do people say 'biblioteca', or a phrase like 'najil ju'un'?
biblioteca.note: Changed from descriptive naajil ju'un. Modern institution; Spanish biblioteca is the likely everyday form, and the naajil- phrase clashed with naaj (casa). Alternative for review: naajil ju'un 'house of paper/books' (naaj + -il + ju'un 'paper, book'), not established, no institutional source.
